name: At home, in the old days
kid: Long ago, the computer phoned the internet! Its modem beeped, whistled and screeched down the phone line, and while you were online, nobody could use the phone. The video trickled back very, very slowly.
nerd: 1990s dial-up: the PC's V.90 modem calls the ISP. The exchange switches the call through the phone network to the ISP's modem bank, and PPP gives the PC its own public address. No Wi‑Fi, no router, no NAT, and about 50 kbit/s on a good line.

describe.kid: The cut-away house has a desk with a computer and an old telephone on a little table. The computer's modem phones the internet company down the phone line to the internet cloud. Requests go out and video creeps back, very slowly.
describe.nerd: The overview of a 1990s home: one computer whose modem dials the ISP over the phone line, which the telephone shares. No LAN, no NAT: PPP runs from the computer to the ISP's gateway. Requests go up, and video comes back at modem speed.

pc.kid: The computer has a modem inside. It dials the internet company’s phone number, then sings your parcel down the phone line as whistles and hisses.
pc.nerd: No router: the modem's PPP link makes the computer itself a host on the internet, with the public address 203.0.113.7 it got from IPCP for this call.

bng.kid: Here your internet company’s modems answer the call. They check your password, give the computer an address and send the parcels on to the internet.
bng.nerd: The ISP's access server: a bank of digital modems on the phone network's trunks. It answers, checks your login (CHAP), assigns an address (IPCP) and routes the PPP session's packets.

internet.nerd: The telephone network (a circuit through the exchange, not part of the internet at all) to the ISP's modem bank, then the ISP's core, then either peering at an IXP or paid transit, ending at a CDN cache. Each shaded area is one operator’s network. This is today’s internet: in 1995 there were no CDNs.
